title: Moon Search

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Where science fiction leads, science sometimes follows. Astronomers are beginning the search for satellites around some of the thousands of known and suspected exoplanets in an effort to find a moon which, like the one in James Cameron’s science fiction film Avatar, is capable of supporting life. Besides the lure of being the first to find something new, there is reason to suspect that if life does exist elsewhere, in places other than Earth, then it might be on the moon of an alien planet.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most organised attempt at the moment to find such a moon is called the Hunt for Exomoons with Kepler. Led by Dr David Kipping of the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics in Massachusetts, USA, it has the advantage that it uses data which have already been collected. Kepler, an orbiting telescope owned by NASA, America’s space agency, looks for exoplanets by identifying the tiny dip in light intensity caused when one of them passes in front of its host star – a phenomenon known as ‘transiting’. So far, 105 planets have been discovered this way and many more have been suggested.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Kipping’s technique relies on the fact that the orbits of moons, especially those which are large compared with their planets, cause the planets’ orbits to 'wobble'. Using Earth as an example, someone looking at the way it moves from afar would be able to deduce the moon’s existence from irregularities in the Earth’s orbit, without having to see it directly. Kipping hopes to see similar gyrations or wobbles in the paths of transiting planets detected by Kepler. This technique has already been used to identify the small movements induced by unseen, non-transiting planets which interfere with the orbits of their transiting brothers. For moons, though, the effects will very probably be minute – right on the ‘very edge’ of what Kepler can detect, says Greg Laughlin, a planet hunter at the University of California, Santa Cruz. He doubts whether Kipping's search will bear fruit in identifying exomoons using this method. However, he acknowledges the soundness of Kipping’s work and supports the theoretical basis for it.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Most of the exoplanets detected so far are much bigger than the Earth, so for moons going around them to be detectable, they would have to be considerably bigger than any moon in our solar system. Specifically, Kipping thinks, they would need to have at least a fifth of the mass of Earth. Ganymede, Jupiter’s most massive satellite, (and also the biggest that is currently available for study), has only a fortieth of the Earth’s mass.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: If Kipping’s approach fails, moon-hunters need not despair. NASA may soon launch a new planet-hunting spacecraft called the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) . Unlike Kepler, which stares fixedly at a single patch of space, TESS would survey the whole sky. Crucially, the stars it is intended to examine are much closer – and appear brighter – than those Kepler is looking at. This makes both plant hunting and moon hunting much easier.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also a hope that the biggest space telescope, the James Webb Space Telescope, could give astronomers the opportunity to take pictures of exomoons directly. In a paper posted online Dr Mary Ann Peters and Dr Edwin Turner, of Princeton University, ponder whether some moons might shine brightly enough to be visible from Earth. Their idea relies on a phenomenon called tidal heating. In the same way that the gravitational pull of Earth’s moon causes tides in the oceans, a planet will tug more strongly on the near sides of its moons than the far sides. These tidal forces knead the inside of the moon, and the resulting friction generates heat. Peters and Turner propose to look for a replicated version of lo, Jupiter’s third largest moon. They have calculated that if a large enough moon, proportionally similar to lo, was orbiting close enough to a planet sufficiently distant from its star for the signal not to be drowned out by starlight, it would give off enough infra-red heat to be visible from Earth – if it were close enough. There is a lot of speculation here but the rewards could be great. In the search for bodies other than Earth that might play host to life, exomoons are good possibilities.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: With Earth as the only example to go from, it is hard to be sure what conditions really favour the development of life. This one example does, however, suggest something which is rocky, possesses an atmosphere, and is warm enough to keep water in liquid form. Such a body does not necessarily have to be a planet, and moons might be more habitable. Small planets close to their parent stars risk becoming tidally locked: that is, the lengths of their days come to match their orbital periods, and they thus have one permanently hot hemisphere and one that is permanently cold. This would probably not be good for the development of life. Though a moon may become tidally locked to its parent star, it will always have some sort of day-night cycle – even if it is an odd one from a terrestrial point of view.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The warmth provided by tidal heating might also help make those moons that are too cold on the surface for water to stay liquid, inhabitable nevertheless. Planetary scientists consider that Enceladus and Europa, which have surface temperatures hundreds of degrees below zero, may have subsurface oceans which are kept liquid by a combination of radioactive decay and tidal heating from Saturn and Jupiter, their respective planets. It is hard to believe that exomoons do not exist. And there is no better way to find something than to look for it.
